title: {1: "a", True: "b"} has only one key in Python, because True equals 1
assumption: A boolean key and an integer key in a dictionary are always distinct entries, since booleans and integers are different types.

input.display: {1: "a", True: "b"}  ->  {1: "b"}, a dict with exactly one entry
input.description: Building a lookup table or counter dict keyed partly by integers and partly by booleans from mixed data (e.g. a CSV or JSON blob where some flag fields were coerced to 0/1 and others stayed as true/false).

what_goes_wrong: Inserting entries keyed `1` and `True` (or `0` and `False`) into the same dict overwrites one with the other instead of creating two entries, silently losing data with no error.
why: `bool` is a subclass of `int` in Python (`class bool(int)`), specifically so that `True` and `1` behave identically wherever an integer is expected. As a consequence, `True == 1` is `True`, and `hash(True) == hash(1)`, and Python dicts (and sets) de-duplicate keys by equality-and-hash together -- so `1` and `True` are, as far as a dict is concerned, the exact same key, and whichever value was assigned last wins.

repros.code:
print(isinstance(True, int), True == 1, hash(True) == hash(1))
print(True + True)  # arithmetic coercion, unsurprising on its own
d = {1: "a", True: "b"}
print(d, len(d))

fix: Never key a dict/set by a mix of booleans and small integers if you need them distinct; normalize flag values to a single consistent type (e.g. always `int`, or always `bool`) before using them as keys.

sources.title: Python docs: Built-in Types -- Mapping Types (dict)

test_cases.note: Any dict-building code keyed by mixed int/bool values should decide explicitly whether 1 and True are the same key.
